newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Mad cow crisis hits Dalgety profits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mad cow crisis hits Dalgety profits.

text.p: Britain's petfood and agribusiness group Dalgety Plc said on Monday the BSE mad cow' disease crisis hit profits last year but it was confident of growth this year despite uncertainties about animal feed.

Dalgety's shares moved higher after the results as the market had been braced for a poor performance and profits were towards the top of expectations. The shares stood nine pence up at 336 pence by mid-morning.

Pre-tax profits excluding exceptional items fell 20 percent to 101.9 million pounds ($159 million) from 127.1 million. Profits including exceptional items -- mainly gains this year from the sale of its snacks and sauces business -- were 89.6 million pounds, down from 93.7 million.
Chief executive Richard Clothier said the year had been exceptionally challenging for the group.
"A steep rise in raw material costs and the BSE crisis seriously affected four of our five businesses," he said in a statement.
Clothier said Dalgety had had a tough start to the current year because the mad cow disease crisis had reduced demand for cattle feed and restricted petfood exports.
But he expected the group's performance would improve for the year as a whole.

"We've still not resumed (petfood) exports entirely and we have this reduction in cattle feed volumes, but despite those two we still expect the year as a whole to show significant growth," he said in a telephone interview.
Analysts were encouraged by Dalgety's confidence in achieving growth this year.
"The company is basically saying it's going to be on the move again after what was an extremely difficult year," said food industry analyst David Lang at Henderson Crosthwaite.

Uncertainty among farmers about how many cattle would be destroyed to wipe out bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) or mad cow disease in Britain had reduced demand for cattle feed by about 20 percent in the past couple of months, Clothier said.
In petfood, Dalgety was still having trouble getting necessary certification required to resume exports to Europe.
Dalgety's food ingredients business, which supplies seasonings to hamburger and sausage makers, was also hit by the BSE. But demand was beginning to build back up, clothier said.
The chief executive said the cost of the mad cow crisis, plus the withdrawal of pet food in the Netherlands, totalled about 20 million pounds.
Earlier this year Dalgety had to recall petfood in the Netherlands after cats died from eating contaminated food.
Petfood in Britain had a disappointing year as the market declined and Dalgety lost market share, particularly in dogfood.
But its main brand Felix, acquired from Quaker Oats last year, became the leading canned catfood brand in the UK, with 26 percent of the market.
The company has just been through a radical reorganisation after selling its snacks, sauces and produce businesses to focus mainly on petfood and agribusiness.

It expanded petfood via a 422 million pound purchase of Quaker Oats Co's European petfood operations just over a year ago. Dalgety said it was pleased with the acquisition and had made progress integrating the two businesses.
